query: For a multi-phase eutectic high-entropy alloy exposed to simultaneous wear and corrosion at elevated temperature, what single mechanistic hypothesis could explain the accelerated coupled degradation and why it occurs? Specify a controlled comparison capable of distinguishing the proposed explanation, predict the changes in total degradation and the individual wear and corrosion responses relative to a matched baseline, define the relevant boundary conditions, identify supporting evidence, and give a clear falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: Rapid thermal cycling induces residual stresses and accentuates micro-galvanic coupling at phase boundaries in the multi-phase eutectic high-entropy alloy, which under simultaneous wear and corrosion at elevated temperature leads to accelerated degradation.
generation.material_initial_state: Multi-phase eutectic high-entropy alloy with distinct phase boundaries and intrinsic microstructural heterogeneity.
generation.intervention: Application of rapid heating–quenching cycles during testing.
generation.conditions: Simultaneous wear and corrosion at elevated temperature in an immersed reciprocating alumina-ball tribocorrosion environment.
generation.structural_mediator: The phase boundaries acting as sites for micro-galvanic cells, whose electrochemical potential differences are intensified by thermal cycling-induced residual stresses and microstructural modifications.
generation.mechanism: The rapid heating–quenching cycles cause localized thermal stresses and microstructural changes that enhance the potential differences between phases. This promotes micro-galvanic corrosion at phase interfaces, while mechanical wear continuously removes any nascent protective films. The interplay between accelerated localized corrosion and wear results in a synergistic, accelerated overall degradation of the material.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to a baseline sample tested isothermally (without rapid heating–quenching), the alloy will show increased total degradation characterized by both higher wear rates (deeper and wider wear tracks) and enhanced localized corrosion (increased corrosion pit density and size).
generation.baseline: The same multi-phase eutectic high-entropy alloy exposed to simultaneous wear and corrosion at elevated temperature under isothermal conditions (constant temperature, no rapid thermal cycling).
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies under conditions of elevated temperature and in corrosive environments that replicate the alumina-ball tribocorrosion setup, specifically with material systems where phase boundary galvanic interactions are significant.
generation.uncertainty: The exact quantitative contribution of thermal cycling versus inherent microstructural heterogeneity to the degradation rate, as well as the magnitude of the synergistic effect between wear and corrosion, remain uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of identical multi-phase eutectic high-entropy alloy samples. Subject one set to simultaneous wear and corrosion tests under elevated temperature with rapid heating–quenching cycles, and the other set to the same wear and corrosion conditions at a constant elevated temperature (isothermal control). All samples should be tested using the immersed reciprocating alumina-ball tribocorrosion benchmarking system, ensuring identical testing durations and environmental conditions.
measurements: Total mass loss after controlled testing duration
Wear track profiles (depth and width) via profilometry or microscopy
Density and size distribution of corrosion pits using SEM/EDS
Electrochemical measurements (such as corrosion potential and current) during tests
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the samples exposed to rapid heating–quenching cycles do not show a statistically significant increase in total degradation, wear track dimensions, and/or localized corrosion features compared to the isothermal control samples, then the hypothesis attributing accelerated degradation to thermal cycling induced micro-galvanic effects is falsified.
